Instructor and TA material. Not rendered into the student site.

## Setup

- **15 envelopes**, each with a printed image of its 6 cards on the outside and,
  inside, the 6 cards, the fact slip and a reference card.
- Groups of 6, TAs filling gaps. ~72 enrolled, so expect about 12 groups.
- **Roles come from the colour of the card each player draws.** Black = Sage
  (truth), red = Trickster (lies). This is the one thing the old materials never
  wrote down, and students cannot play without it.
- The card image is public, so **the Trickster count is public too** --- count the
  reds. Say this; without it the all-Sage and all-Trickster readings are
  indistinguishable.

## Rules --- as printed on the cards

1. Sages answer truthfully. Tricksters always answer falsely.
2. **Two info rounds.** Each round every player asks one yes/no question;
   everyone answers about their own card.
3. **Debate round.** Compare answers and look for contradictions.
4. **Conclusion.** Agree on everyone's roles, then reveal.

The **fact slips are decorative**: the six cards are printed on the envelope, so
anything true of them is already public and the fact adds no information. Harmless
to leave in; nothing depends on them.

**One defect.** The to-do list offered Packet 12 a second fact, *"all spade cards
are even."* It is ill-defined --- the only spade is Q♠ and a Queen is neither even
nor odd. If that is the slip in the envelope, swap it for the kings-and-queens one.

Packets 11 and 14 have a single Trickster and 12 has five. All are playable;
they just run fast or strange. Packet 12 is worth calling on in the debrief,
since with five liars a majority vote gives that group confidently the wrong
answer.

## Driving the debrief

Two questions are dead, and both are worth letting them discover:

| Question | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "Is your card red?" | everyone says no | a black card isn't red and says so; a red card is and denies it |
| "Is your card black?" | everyone says yes | the same collapse, inverted |

With twelve questions available, burning one on these costs nothing and makes
the point better than any warning would.

Then drive the discussion from the **Lying is an operator** slide. Reveal the
right column one fragment at a time and let them supply the last step. The
answer to reach: ask about a property whose value you already know for that
person. That fixes the "has it" column, leaving two rows that differ in the
output --- so their answer reports the lie bit directly.

Either value works. Fix the column to 0 and a "yes" means lying; fix it to 1 and
a "no" means lying. If a group offers one direction, ask for the other.

Known-false is much easier to find in practice: after a "yes" the surviving
cards are (black with the property) together with (red without it), spanning both
colours, so naming a suit or rank none of them has is easy while finding
something they all share is rare.

## Next year

**Grouping was the weak point in 2026W1.** Forming groups of exactly six in a
fixed-seat lecture hall cost time and never quite worked.

It does not have to be six. Checked across five packets with two questions:
groups of **4, 5 and 6 all solve uniquely**. Each player's answers pin down their
own card's colour independently, so cards left undealt in the envelope create no
ambiguity about anyone who is holding one.

So next year, do not form groups at all:

- Hand one envelope to each **block of adjacent seats** --- roughly six wide, but
  whatever the row gives you.
- Deal one card per person present; leftovers stay in the envelope.
- Nobody moves, nothing is counted off, and it absorbs whatever attendance is.

Two consequences to state if you do this:

- Say that **not every printed card is necessarily in play**, or students will
  reason about a card nobody holds.
- The red count on the envelope becomes an **upper bound** on the number of
  Tricksters rather than the exact figure. The puzzle does not need the exact
  count, so this costs nothing --- but do not tell them to count the reds.

## Handoff

Two claims about the room, both established during the game:

- *"Priya is a Trickster"* --- settled by finding a contradiction. Certain.
- *"Most questions were about the same card"* --- settled by counting. Supported.

Both are arguments. This course is the first kind. Do not oversell the
connection; it gets earned in lecture 3, when a boolean mask turns out to be a
predicate evaluated over rows.
